overview.text: The Hall effect is the appearance of a voltage across the sides of a material carrying electric current when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to that current. The magnetic force deflects moving charge carriers sideways; their buildup on one side creates a transverse voltage called the Hall voltage. In a suitable measurement setup, its polarity can help identify whether electrons or positively charged holes dominate conduction, and its size can help determine carrier concentration. Hall sensors use the effect to detect magnetic fields. Edwin Hall observed it in 1879 in experiments with current-carrying gold foil at Johns Hopkins; semiconductor technology later helped make the effect useful in practical sensors.

key_facts.text: The Hall voltage runs across the material, perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.
In appropriately arranged semiconductor measurements, Hall-voltage polarity can indicate whether electrons or holes are the main charge carriers.
Measuring Hall voltage alongside known current and magnetic field can help determine semiconductor charge-carrier density.
Hall sensors use the effect to measure magnetic fields; the same principle underlies sensors used in many settings.
Edwin Hall observed the effect in 1879 using a current-carrying strip of gold foil at Johns Hopkins University.
